title: حِكَايَةُ الثَّعْلَبِ وَالْغُرَابِ
part: Night 151 · The Fox and the Crow, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 751–753 (Night 151, continuing directly from nights-150), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 151 continues the tale of the fox and the crow. The fox finishes his fable of the flea and the mouse: the mouse takes the flea in as a friend, and when the merchant brings home a heap of dinars and sleeps on them, the flea bites him until he leaves his bed for the bench outside, and the mouse carries off every coin. So, says the fox, a kindness done to him will be repaid. The crow is not persuaded: kindness is no debt owed to an enemy, and the fox has lately betrayed his own companion the wolf; how could the crow trust him? He begins a fable of his own, about a tyrannical falcon, which breaks off at dawn. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the first-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-first night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiya, “the first”, is the ordinal used for “one” inside a compound number; it is feminine to agree with layla. al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْفَأْرَةَ لَمَّا سَمِعَتْ كَلَامَ الْبُرْغُوثِ قَالَتْ إِذَا كَانَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَى مَا رَسَمْتَ وَأَخْبَرْتَ فَاطْمَئِنَّ هُنَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-faʾrata lammā samiʿat kalāma al-burghūthi qālat idhā kāna al-kalāmu ʿalā mā rasamta wa-akhbarta fa-iṭmaʾinna hunā
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the mouse, when she heard the speech of the flea, said: If the matter is according-to what you-have-set-out and told, then be-at-rest here;
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the mouse heard what the flea said, she answered, “If things are as you have set them out and told them, then rest easy here;
sentences.n: The night opens by repeating the words on which the last one broke off. rasama, “to trace, lay down”: here “as you have set it out”. fa-iṭmaʾinna, “then be at ease”, the imperative of iṭmaʾanna; the shadda in فاطمئنّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَمَا عَلَيْكَ إِلَّا مَطَرُ السَّلَامَةِ وَلَا تَجِدُ إِلَّا مَا يَسُرُّكَ وَلَا يُصِيبُكَ إِلَّا مَا يُصِيبُنِي
sentences.tr: wa-mā ʿalayka illā maṭaru al-salāmati wa-lā tajidu illā mā yasurruka wa-lā yuṣībuka illā mā yuṣībunī
sentences.l: and nothing (is) upon-you but the rain of the safety; and you-will-not find but what gladdens-you, and nothing will-befall-you but what befalls-me.
sentences.i: nothing will fall upon you here but a rain of safety; you will meet with nothing but what pleases you, and nothing will befall you that does not befall me too.
sentences.n: mā ʿalayka illā …, “there is nothing upon you but …”. maṭar al-salāma, “the rain of safety”, is an unusual figure: read as “nothing will come down on you but well-being”. Rain is the stock Arabic image of bounty and mercy, which makes the figure less strange than it looks; still, the phrase is not a usual one, the reading is not certain, and maṭar may be corrupt. It is kept as printed. The shaddas in the first two الّا and in يسرّك are the print's own; the third illā is printed without one.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ بَذَلْتُ لَكَ مَوَدَّتِي وَلَا تَنْدَمْ عَلَى مَا فَاتَكَ مِنْ دَمِ التَّاجِرِ وَلَا تَأْسَفْ عَلَى قُوتِكَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qad badhaltu laka mawaddatī wa-lā tandam ʿalā mā fātaka min dami al-tājiri wa-lā taʾsaf ʿalā qūtika minhu
sentences.l: And I-have given-freely to-you my-affection; and do-not regret what has-escaped-you of the blood of the merchant, and do-not grieve over your-food from-him.
sentences.i: I have given you my friendship freely. Do not regret the merchant's blood that you have lost, and do not grieve for the living you drew from him.
sentences.n: badhala, “to give freely, offer”. fāta, “to slip past, be lost to someone”. qūt, “food, daily sustenance”: the merchant's blood was the flea's food.

sentences.t: وَارْضَ بِمَا تَيَسَّرَ لَكَ بِبُلْغَةٍ مِنَ الْعَيْشِ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ أَسْلَمُ لَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-irḍa bi-mā tayassara laka bi-bulghatin mina al-ʿayshi fa-inna dhālika aslamu laka
sentences.l: And be-content with what has-come-easy to-you, with a bare-sufficiency of the living; for that (is) safer for-you.
sentences.i: Be content with whatever comes easily to you, with just enough to live on; that is the safer course for you.
sentences.n: raḍiya bi-, “to be content with”: the verb chooses bi-, and irḍa is its imperative. bulgha, “just enough to get by on”: the second bi- restates the first, “with what is easy, that is, with a bare sufficiency”. aslam, “safer”, the comparative of salīm.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَمِعْتُ أَيُّهَا الْبُرْغُوثُ بَعْضَ الشُّعَرَاءِ مِنَ الْوُعَّاظِ يَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qad samiʿtu ayyuhā al-burghūthu baʿḍa al-shuʿarāʾi mina al-wuʿʿāẓi yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: And I-have heard, O flea, one of the poets, of the preachers, saying these verses. Verse:
sentences.i: I have heard one of the poets who preach, O flea, recite these lines:
sentences.n: wuʿʿāẓ, “preachers, admonishers”, plural of wāʿiẓ: the poet is one who preaches. شعر, “verse”, is the print's rubric announcing the poem.

sentences.t:
سَلَكْتُ الْقَنَاعَةَ وَالْاِنْفِرَادَ * وَقَضَّيْتُ دَهْرِي بِمَاذَا اتَّفَقْ
بِكَسْرَةِ خُبْزٍ وَشِرْبَةِ مَاءٍ * وَمِلْحٍ جَرِيشٍ وَثَوْبٍ خَلِقْ
فَاِنْ يَسَّرَ اللّٰهُ فِي عِيْشَتِيْ * وَاِلَّا قَنَعْتُ بِمَا قَدْ رُزِقْ
sentences.tr:
salaktu al-qanāʿata wa-al-infirāda * wa-qaḍḍaytu dahrī bi-mādhā ittafaq
bi-kasrati khubzin wa-shirbati māʾin * wa-milḥin jarīshin wa-thawbin khaliq
fa-in yassara allāhu fī ʿīshatī * wa-illā qanaʿtu bi-mā qad ruziq
sentences.l:
I-have-travelled-the-road-of contentment and the keeping-apart, and spent my-lifetime with whatever chanced:
with a broken-piece of bread and a draught of water, and salt, coarse-ground, and a garment worn-out.
So if God makes-easy in my-living — and if-not, I-am-content with what has been-provided.
sentences.i:
I have walked the road of contentment and of keeping to myself, and passed my days on whatever came my way:
a crust of bread, a drink of water, coarse salt and a threadbare robe.
If God should ease my living, well and good; if not, I am content with what I have been given.
sentences.n: The rhyme falls on -aq/-iq, with the final vowel silenced for the rhyme (ittafaq, khaliq, ruziq). salaka, “to travel a road”: to make a thing one's way of life. qaḍḍā dahrahu, “to spend one's lifetime”. bi-mādhā ittafaq, “with whatever happened to come”. kisra, “a broken piece”, of bread; shirba, “a single drink”. jarīsh, “coarsely ground”; khaliq, “worn, threadbare”. ʿīsha, “manner of living”: the print gives its yāʾ a sukūn (عِيْشَتِيْ), its way of marking a long ī. The first condition, “if God makes it easy”, has no answer: “well and good” is understood. ruziq, passive, “has been granted (as provision)”. The print points qanaʿtu; Classical usage keeps qaniʿa, “to be content”, apart from qanaʿa, “to ask humbly”, but the sense here is plainly contentment. The verse hamza is pointed as a bare alif with its vowel (فَاِنْ, وَاِلَّا, وَالْاِنْفِرَادَ), as the print does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْبُرْغُوثُ كَلَامَ الْفَأْرَةِ قَالَ يَا أُخْتِي قَدْ سَمِعْتُ وَصِيَّتَكِ وَأَنَا مُنْقَادٌ إِلَى طَاعَتِكِ وَلَا قُوَّةَ لِي عَلَى مُخَالَفَتِكِ إِلَى أَنْ يَنْقَضِيَ الْعُمْرُ بِتِلْكَ النِّيَّةِ الْحَسَنَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-burghūthu kalāma al-faʾrati qāla yā ukhtī qad samiʿtu waṣiyyataki wa-anā munqādun ilā ṭāʿatiki wa-lā quwwata lī ʿalā mukhālafatiki ilā an yanqaḍiya al-ʿumru bi-tilka al-niyyati al-ḥasanati
sentences.l: And when the flea heard the speech of the mouse, he said: O my-sister, I-have heard your-counsel, and I (am) led to your-obedience, and (there is) no strength for-me against opposing-you, until the life is-ended, with that intention, the good.
sentences.i: When the flea heard what the mouse said, it answered, “Sister, I have heard your counsel and I yield to your bidding; I have no power to go against you, and so it shall be, in that good intent, until my life is done.”
sentences.n: waṣiyya, “counsel, charge”. munqād ilā, “led to, submissive to”. lā quwwata lī ʿalā, “I have no strength for”: lā of absolute negation. inqaḍā, “to come to an end”. bi-tilka al-niyya, “with that intention”: the bi- says in what spirit he will obey.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْفَأْرَةُ كَفَى بِصِدْقِ الْمَوَدَّةِ صَلَاحَ النِّيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-faʾratu kafā bi-ṣidqi al-mawaddati ṣalāḥa al-niyyati
sentences.l: And the mouse said to-him: Sufficient-is the truth of the affection (for) the soundness of the intention.
sentences.i: The mouse said to him, “True affection is all that a sound intention needs.”
sentences.n: kafā bi-…, “… is enough”: the bi- only marks the subject, as in kafā bi-llāhi shahīdan, “God suffices as witness”. ṣalāḥa al-niyya is read as the object of kafā, “it is enough for” (kafāhu, “it sufficed him”). On the pattern of kafā bi-llāhi shahīdan the accusative may instead fill the “as …” slot: “sincere affection is sound intention enough”, that is, true friendship is itself the good intent the flea has promised. The saying is compressed and the reading is not certain; ṣalāḥu al-niyya, “sound intention is enough, with sincere affection”, is also possible.

sentences.t: فَاتَّصَلَ الْوُدُّ وَانْعَقَدَ بَيْنَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ittaṣala al-wuddu wa-inʿaqada baynahumā
sentences.l: So the love was-joined and was-knotted between-the-two-of-them.
sentences.i: So affection grew up between them and the bond was tied.
sentences.n: ittaṣala, “to be joined, run on unbroken”; inʿaqada, “to be knotted, concluded”, of a pact. The shadda in الودّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْبُرْغُوثُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ يَأْوِي إِلَى فِرَاشِ التَّاجِرِ وَلَا يَتَجَاوَزُ بُلْغَتَهُ وَيَأْوِي بِالنَّهَارِ مَعَ الْفَأْرَةِ فِي مَسْكَنِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-burghūthu baʿda dhālika yaʾwī ilā firāshi al-tājiri wa-lā yatajāwazu bulghatahu wa-yaʾwī bi-al-nahāri maʿa al-faʾrati fī maskanihā
sentences.l: And the flea after that used-to-resort to the bed of the merchant, and did-not go-beyond his-bare-sufficiency, and lodged by the day with the mouse in her-dwelling.
sentences.i: After that the flea would go to the merchant's bed, taking no more than it needed to live on, and by day it would shelter with the mouse in her home.
sentences.n: kāna with an imperfect, “used to”, of habit. awā ilā, “to resort to, take shelter in”. bulgha, again: “just enough to live on”. bi-al-nahār, “by day”: bi- of time.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّ التَّاجِرَ جَاءَ لَيْلَةً إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ بِدَنَانِيرَ كَثِيرَةٍ فَجَعَلَ يُقَلِّبُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa anna al-tājira jāʾa laylatan ilā manzilihi bi-danānīra kathīratin fa-jaʿala yuqallibuhā
sentences.l: And it-chanced that the merchant came one-night to his-house with many dinars, and he-began turning-them-over.
sentences.i: Now it happened that one night the merchant came home with a great many dinars and set about turning them over in his hands.
sentences.n: jāʾa bi-, “to come with, bring”: the verb chooses bi-. danānīr, plural of dīnār, takes no tanwīn and ends in -a after a preposition. jaʿala with an imperfect, “he began to”. qallaba, “to turn over and over”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْفَأْرَةُ صَوْتَ الدَّنَانِيرِ أَطْلَعَتْ رَأْسَهَا مِنْ جُحْرِهَا وَجَعَلَتْ تَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا حَتَّى وَضَعَهَا التَّاجِرُ تَحْتَ وِسَادَةٍ وَنَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-faʾratu ṣawta al-danānīri aṭlaʿat raʾsahā min juḥrihā wa-jaʿalat tanẓuru ilayhā ḥattā waḍaʿahā al-tājiru taḥta wisādatin wa-nāma
sentences.l: And when the mouse heard the sound of the dinars, she made-appear her-head from her-hole and began looking at-them, until the merchant put-them under a cushion and slept.
sentences.i: When the mouse heard the chink of the dinars, she put her head out of her hole and watched them, until the merchant laid them under a pillow and went to sleep.
sentences.n: aṭlaʿa, “to make appear, put out”. juḥr, “burrow, hole”. wisāda, “pillow, cushion”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْفَأْرَةُ لِلْبُرْغُوثِ أَمَا تَرَى الْفُرْصَةَ الْمُمَكَّنَةَ وَالْحَظَّ الْعَظِيمَ فَهَلْ عِنْدَكَ حِيلَةٌ تُوصِلُنَا إِلَى بُلُوغِ الْغَرَضِ مِنْ تِلْكَ الدَّنَانِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-faʾratu li-al-burghūthi a-mā tarā al-furṣata al-mumakkanata wa-al-ḥaẓẓa al-ʿaẓīma fa-hal ʿindaka ḥīlatun tūṣilunā ilā bulūghi al-gharaḍi min tilka al-danānīri
sentences.l: And the mouse said to the flea: Do-you not see the opportunity, the made-possible, and the fortune, the great? So is (there) with-you a device (that) brings-us to the attaining of the aim from those dinars?
sentences.i: The mouse said to the flea, “Do you not see the chance that lies within our reach, and what great good fortune it is? Have you some trick that will bring us to our goal with those dinars?”
sentences.n: a-mā, “do … not?”, a question expecting yes. The shadda in الممكّنة is the print's own; the word is read mumakkana, “made possible, put within reach”, though mumakkina, “giving the power”, would also fit. ḥīla, “a stratagem”. awṣala ilā, “to bring to”. gharaḍ, “aim, object of desire”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْبُرْغُوثُ إِنَّهُ لَا يَحْسُنُ لِمَنْ طَلَبَ الْغَرَضَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ قَادِرًا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-burghūthu innahu lā yaḥsunu li-man ṭalaba al-gharaḍa illā an yakūna qādiran ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And the flea said: Truly it (is so): it-is-not fitting for whoever seeks the aim, except that he be able for-it.
sentences.i: The flea said, “It is not fitting for anyone to pursue an aim unless he has the power to reach it.
sentences.n: innahu, “truly it is the case that”: the -hu is the pronoun of the fact (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) and points ahead to the clause. ḥasuna li-, “to be fitting for”. qādir ʿalā, “able to do”.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ كَانَ ضَعِيفًا عَنْهُ وَقَعَ فِيمَا يَحْذَرُهُ وَلَمْ يُدْرِكْ مُرَادَهُ مَعَ الضَّعْفِ وَإِنِ اسْتَحْكَمَتْ قُوَّةُ الْمُحْتَالِ كَالْعُصْفُورِ الَّذِى يَلْتَقِطُ الْحَبَّ فَيَقَعُ فِى الشَّبَكَةِ فَيَقْتَنِصُهُ صَائِدُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-in kāna ḍaʿīfan ʿanhu waqaʿa fīmā yaḥdharuhu wa-lam yudrik murādahu maʿa al-ḍaʿfi wa-ini istaḥkamat quwwatu al-muḥtāli ka-al-ʿuṣfūri alladhī yaltaqiṭu al-ḥabba fa-yaqaʿu fī al-shabakati fa-yaqtaniṣuhu ṣāʾiduhu
sentences.l: For if he is weak for-it, he-falls into what he-guards-against, and does-not attain his-desire with the weakness, even-if the strength of the schemer be-made-firm — like the sparrow which picks-up the grain, and falls into the net, and its-hunter snares-it.
sentences.i: For if he is too weak for it, he falls into the very thing he fears and, weak as he is, never gains his end, however well-founded the schemer's strength may be: like the sparrow that pecks up the grain and falls into the net, and the fowler takes it.
sentences.n: ḍaʿīf ʿan, “too weak for”. ḥadhira, “to beware of, dread”. wa-in istaḥkamat quwwatu al-muḥtāl, “even if the schemer's strength be made fast”: the clause is compressed and its point is not certain; it is read as “however well he schemes”, cunning without strength will not serve. ka-, “like”, introduces the comparison. iltaqaṭa, “to pick up”; iqtanaṣa, “to snare”; ṣāʾid, “hunter, fowler”. The print spells الذى and فى with a final ى.

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ لَكِ قُوَّةٌ عَلَى أَخْذِ الدَّنَانِيرِ وَلَا عَلَى إِخْرَاجِهَا مِنَ الْبَيْتِ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa laki quwwatun ʿalā akhdhi al-danānīri wa-lā ʿalā ikhrājihā mina al-bayti
sentences.l: And there-is-not for-you strength for taking the dinars, nor for bringing-them-out from the house;
sentences.i: You have not the strength to take the dinars, nor to get them out of the house;
sentences.n: laki, “to you”, feminine: the flea is speaking to the mouse. quwwa ʿalā, “strength for, power to do”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا لَاطَاقَةَ لِي عَلَى ذَلِكَ بَلْ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ عَلَى حَمْلِ دِينَارٍ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-anā lā ṭāqata lī ʿalā dhālika bal wa-lā aqdiru ʿalā ḥamli dīnārin wāḥidin minhā
sentences.l: and I — no power for-me over that; nay, and I-am-not-able (even) to carry one dinar of-them.
sentences.i: and as for me, I have no strength for it; why, I could not carry so much as a single dinar of them.
sentences.n: lā ṭāqata lī, “I have no power”, lā of absolute negation: the print runs lā and ṭāqa together (لاطاقة). bal wa-lā, “nay, not even”. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”.

sentences.t: فَأَنْتِ وَشَأْنُكِ بِالدَّنَانِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-anti wa-shaʾnuki bi-al-danānīri
sentences.l: So you and your-affair with the dinars.
sentences.i: So the dinars are your affair: do with them as you will.”
sentences.n: anta wa-shaʾnuka, “you and your business”: an idiom for leaving someone to do as they please. bi-, “with”, here “as regards”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْفَأْرَهُ إِنِّي أَعْدَدْتُ فِي جُحْرِي هَذَا سَبْعِينَ مَنْفَذًا أَخْرُجُ مِنْهُ إِذَا طَلَبْتُ الْخُرُوجَ وَأَعْدَدْتُ لِلذَّخَائِرِ مَوْضِعًا حَرِيزًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-faʾratu innī aʿdadtu fī juḥrī hādhā sabʿīna manfadhan akhruju minhu idhā ṭalabtu al-khurūja wa-aʿdadtu li-al-dhakhāʾiri mawḍiʿan ḥarīzan
sentences.l: And the mouse said to him: Indeed-I have-prepared in this my-hole seventy outlets, (each) I-go-out by-it when I-seek the going-out; and I-have-prepared for the stores a place secure.
sentences.i: The mouse said to him, “I have made seventy ways out of this hole of mine, to leave by whenever I want to go out, and I have made a safe place for my stores.
sentences.n: The print spells al-faʾra with a final ه for ة (الفأره); the hamza on its alif is the print's own. manfadh, “an outlet, a way through”. akhruju minhu, “I go out by it”, is an unmarked relative clause on the outlets: the singular minhu agrees with the singular manfadhan that counts them. dhakhāʾir, plural of dhakhīra, “a thing laid up, a store, a treasure”; the hamza in للذخائر is the print's own. ḥarīz, “well-guarded, secure”.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ تَحَيَّلْتَ أَنْتَ وَأَخْرَجْتَهُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ فَلَسْتُ أَشُكُّ فِى الظَّفَرِ إِنْ سَاعَدَنِي الْقَدَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-in taḥayyalta anta wa-akhrajtahu mina al-bayti fa-lastu ashukku fī al-ẓafari in sāʿadanī al-qadaru
sentences.l: And if you-contrive, you, and make-him-go-out from the house, then I-am-not doubting about the success, if the decree helps-me.
sentences.i: If you can find some trick to drive him out of the house, I have no doubt that I shall succeed, if fate is on my side.”
sentences.n: taḥayyala, “to use a stratagem, contrive”; the -hu of akhrajtahu is the merchant. ẓafar, “victory; gaining one's end”. فى, with ى for ي, is the print's spelling of fī.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْبُرْغُوثُ قَدِ الْتَزَمْتُ لَكِ بِإِخْرَاجِهِ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-burghūthu qadi iltazamtu laki bi-ikhrājihi mina al-bayti
sentences.l: And the flea said to her: I-have bound-myself to-you to his-expulsion from the house.
sentences.i: The flea said to her, “I take it upon myself to get him out of the house for you.”
sentences.n: iltazama bi-, “to take upon oneself, undertake”: the verb chooses the bi-.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ انْطَلَقَ الْبُرْغُوثُ إِلَى فِرَاشِ التَّاجِرِ وَلَدَغَهُ لَدْغَةً مُفْزِعَةً لَمْ يَكُنْ تَقَدَّمَ مِنْهُ لِلتَّاجِرِ مِثْلُهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inṭalaqa al-burghūthu ilā firāshi al-tājiri wa-ladaghahu ladghatan mufziʿatan lam yakun taqaddama minhu li-al-tājiri mithluhā
sentences.l: Then the flea went-off to the bed of the merchant and bit-him a bite startling, (of which) its-like had-not gone-before from-him to-the-merchant.
sentences.i: Then the flea went off to the merchant's bed and gave him a startling bite, the like of which it had never given him before.
sentences.n: ladagha, “to sting, bite”, of insects and snakes; ladgha, “a bite”, is its noun of single action, used here as an internal object. mufziʿ, “frightening, making one start up”. lam yakun taqaddama, “had not gone before”, a pluperfect. The shadda in تقدّم is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَتَنَحَّى الْبُرْغُوثُ إِلَى مَوْضِعٍ يَأْمَنُ فِيهِ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ مِنَ التَّاجِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-tanaḥḥā al-burghūthu ilā mawḍiʿin yaʾmanu fīhi ʿalā nafsihi mina al-tājiri
sentences.l: And the flea moved-aside to a place (where) it-is-safe in-it for itself from the merchant.
sentences.i: Then the flea drew off to a place where it would be safe from the merchant.
sentences.n: tanaḥḥā, “to move aside, withdraw”. amina ʿalā nafsihi min, “to feel safe for oneself from”. The hamza in يأمن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبَهَ التَّاجِرُ يَطْلُبُهُ فَلَمْ يَجِدْهُ فَرَقَدَ عَلَى جَنْبِهِ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-intabaha al-tājiru yaṭlubuhu fa-lam yajidhu fa-raqada ʿalā janbihi al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the merchant woke, seeking-it, and did-not find-it; so he-lay-down on his-side the other.
sentences.i: The merchant woke and looked for it, but could not find it, so he lay down on his other side.
sentences.n: intabaha, “to wake up”. yaṭlubuhu, “seeking it”, describes how he woke (a circumstantial clause). raqada, “to lie down to sleep”. The madda in الآخر is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَدَغَهُ الْبُرْغُوثُ لَدْغَةً أَشَدَّ مِنَ الْأُولَى فَقَلِقَ التَّاجِرُ وَفَارَقَ مَضْجَعَهُ وَخَرَجَ إِلَى مِصْطَبَةٍ عَلَى بَابِ دَارِهِ فَنَامَ هُنَاكَ وَلَمْ يَنْتَبِهْ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-ladaghahu al-burghūthu ladghatan ashadda mina al-ūlā fa-qaliqa al-tājiru wa-fāraqa maḍjaʿahu wa-kharaja ilā miṣṭabatin ʿalā bābi dārihi fa-nāma hunāka wa-lam yantabih ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And the flea bit-him a bite harder than the first; so the merchant became-restless and left his-lying-place and went-out to a bench at the door of his-house, and slept there and did-not wake until the morning.
sentences.i: Then the flea bit him harder than the first time, and the merchant grew restless, left his bed and went out to a bench by the door of his house; there he slept, and did not wake till morning.
sentences.n: qaliqa, “to be restless, unable to settle”. maḍjaʿ, “a place of lying down, a bed”. miṣṭaba, “a stone bench”, the raised seat built against the front of a house. ilā al-ṣabāḥ, “until the morning”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْفَأْرَهَ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَى نَقْلِ الدَّنَانِيرِ حَتَّى لَمْ تَتْرُكْ مِنْهَا شَيْأً
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-faʾrata aqbalat ʿalā naqli al-danānīri ḥattā lam tatruk minhā shayʾan
sentences.l: Then indeed the mouse set-to on the carrying of the dinars, until she-did-not leave of-them a thing.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the mouse set about carrying off the dinars, until she had left not a single one.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn to, set about” a task. naqala, “to move, carry from place to place”. dīnār, a gold coin. The print again writes al-faʾra with ه, and shayʾan as شيأ, with its hamza on an alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ صَارَ التَّاجِرُ يَتَّهِمُ النَّاسَ وَيَظُنُّ الظُّنُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu ṣāra al-tājiru yattahimu al-nāsa wa-yaẓunnu al-ẓunūna
sentences.l: And when the morning dawned, the merchant began suspecting the people and thinking the thoughts.
sentences.i: When morning came, the merchant began to suspect everyone and to imagine all manner of things.”
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥ, “the morning came”. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to”. ittahama, “to suspect, accuse”. ẓanna al-ẓunūn, “to think thoughts”, to be full of suspicions. The shaddas in فلمّا, يتّهم and النّاس are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ لِلْغُرَابِ وَاعْلَمْ أَنِّي لَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ أَيُّهَا الْغُرَابُ الْبَصِيرُ الْعَاقِلُ الْخَبِيرُ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَصِلَ إِلَيْكَ جَزَاءُ إِحْسَانِكَ إِلَيَّ كَمَا وَصَلَ لِلْفَأْرَةِ جَزَاءُ إِحْسَانِهَا إِلَى الْبُرْغُوثِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla al-thaʿlabu li-al-ghurābi wa-iʿlam annī lam aqul laka hādhā al-kalāma ayyuhā al-ghurābu al-baṣīru al-ʿāqilu al-khabīru illā li-ajli an yaṣila ilayka jazāʾu iḥsānika ilayya kamā waṣala li-al-faʾrati jazāʾu iḥsānihā ilā al-burghūthi
sentences.l: Then the fox said to the crow: And know that I-did-not say to-you this speech, O crow, the clear-sighted, the intelligent, the well-informed, except for the sake that should-reach to-you the requital of your-doing-good to-me, as reached to-the-mouse the requital of her-doing-good to the flea.
sentences.i: Then the fox said to the crow, “Know, O crow — keen-sighted, wise and experienced as you are — that I told you this only so that the reward of your kindness to me might come back to you, as the reward of her kindness to the flea came back to the mouse.
sentences.n: The fox's fable ends, and he turns to its moral. baṣīr, ʿāqil, khabīr, “clear-sighted, intelligent, well-informed”, heaped up in flattery. li-ajli an, “for the sake of, so that”. waṣala li-, “to reach someone”, where Classical prefers ilā; the sentence uses both. Here al-faʾra is spelled with ة (للفأرة); in this night the print uses ة and ه for it interchangeably. The shadda in اليّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَانْظُرْ كَيْفَ جَازَاهَا وَكَافَأَهَا بِأَحْسَنِ الْمُكَافَأَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-unẓur kayfa jāzāhā wa-kāfaʾahā bi-aḥsani al-mukāfaʾati
sentences.l: So look how he-repaid-her and requited-her with the best of the requital.
sentences.i: See how it repaid her, and rewarded her with the finest of rewards.”
sentences.n: jāzā and kāfaʾa, “to repay, requite”, a pair of near-synonyms; the subject is the flea (burghūth is masculine). The hamzas in وكافأها and المكافأة are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْغُرَابُ إِنْ شَاءَ الْمُحْسِنُ يُحْسِنُ أَوْلَا يُحْسِنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ghurābu in shāʾa al-muḥsinu yuḥsinu aw lā yuḥsinu
sentences.l: And the crow said: If the doer-of-good wishes, he-does-good, or he-does-not do-good;
sentences.i: The crow said, “The doer of good does good if he chooses, or else he does not;
sentences.n: The sense: kindness is a free gift, not a debt. After a past-tense condition (in shāʾa) the answer may stand in the indicative, yuḥsinu, instead of the jussive. The print runs aw and lā together (اولا).

sentences.t: وَلَيْسَ الْإِحْسَانُ وَاجِبًا لِمَنِ الْتَمَسَ صِلَةً بِقَطِيعَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-laysa al-iḥsānu wājiban li-mani iltamasa ṣilatan bi-qaṭīʿatin
sentences.l: and the doing-good is not binding toward-whoever seeks a joining with a severing.
sentences.i: and kindness is not owed to one who seeks a bond while bringing estrangement.
sentences.n: ṣila, “a joining; a gift or kindness that binds”, and qaṭīʿa, “a cutting off, estrangement”, are a stock pair of opposites. The li- marks the one to whom the kindness would be owed. The force of bi- here is not certain: “with, along with” (seeking a bond while being an enemy) or “in exchange for” (asking kindness in return for hostility); the second is perhaps the likelier, with the bi- of price, as in ishtarā bi-, “to buy for”; either way the crow means the fox.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ أَحْسَنْتُ إِلَيْكَ مَعَ كَوْنِكَ عَدُوِّي أَكُونُ قَدْ تَسَبَّبْتُ فِي قَطِيعَةِ نَفْسِي
sentences.tr: wa-in aḥsantu ilayka maʿa kawnika ʿaduwwī akūnu qad tasabbabtu fī qaṭīʿati nafsī
sentences.l: And if I-do-good to-you, with your-being my-enemy, I-shall-be (one who) has caused the cutting-off of myself.
sentences.i: If I am kind to you, though you are my enemy, I shall have brought about my own undoing.
sentences.n: aḥsana ilā, “to do good to”. maʿa kawnika, “with your being”, that is, “although you are”. akūnu qad tasabbabtu, “I shall have caused”, a future perfect; akūnu is again indicative in the answer to a past-tense condition. tasabbaba fī, “to be the cause of”. qaṭīʿat nafsī, “the cutting off of myself”, my ruin. The ḍamma on احسنتُ is the print's own; it marks “I”.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ أَيُّهَا الثَّعْلَبُ ذُو مَكْرٍ وَخِدَاعٍ وَمَنْ شِيمَتُهُ الْمَكْرُ وَالْخَدِيعَةُ لَا يُؤْمَنُ عَلَى عَهْدٍ وَمَنْ لَا يُؤْمَنُ عَلَى عَهْدٍ لَا أَمَانَ لَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-anta ayyuhā al-thaʿlabu dhū makrin wa-khidāʿin wa-man shīmatuhu al-makru wa-al-khadīʿatu lā yuʾmanu ʿalā ʿahdin wa-man lā yuʾmanu ʿalā ʿahdin lā amāna lahu
sentences.l: And you, O fox, (are) possessor of guile and deceit; and whoever his-nature (is) the guile and the deception is-not trusted upon a pact; and whoever is-not trusted upon a pact, no safety (is) to-him.
sentences.i: And you, fox, are a creature of guile and deceit; one whose nature is guile and trickery cannot be trusted to keep a pact, and with one who cannot be trusted to keep a pact there is no safety.
sentences.n: dhū, “possessor of”, makes “a creature of guile”. shīma, “natural disposition, character”. amina ʿalā, “to trust someone with”; yuʾmanu is its passive. lā amāna lahu, “there is no safety for him”, nobody is safe with him. The marks on ومَنْ and the hamza in يؤمن are the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ بَلَغَنِي عَنْكَ مِنْ قَرِيبٍ أَنَّكَ غَدَرْتَ بِصَاحِبٍ لَكَ وَهُوَ الذِّئْبُ وَمَكَرْتَ بِهِ حَتَّى أَهْلَكْتَهُ بِغَدْرِكَ وَحِيلَتِكَ وَفَعَلْتَ بِهِ هَذِةِ الْأُمُورَ مَعَ أَنَّهُ مِنْ جِنْسِكَ وَقَدْ صَحَبْتَهُ مُدَّةً مَدِيدَةً فَمَا أَبْقَيْتَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad balaghanī ʿanka min qarībin annaka ghadarta bi-ṣāḥibin laka wa-huwa al-dhiʾbu wa-makarta bihi ḥattā ahlaktahu bi-ghadrika wa-ḥīlatika wa-faʿalta bihi hādhihi al-umūra maʿa annahu min jinsika wa-qad ṣaḥabtahu muddatan madīdatan fa-mā abqayta ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And it-has-reached-me about-you from near that you betrayed a companion of-yours — and he (is) the wolf — and plotted against-him until you-destroyed-him by your-treachery and your-trickery, and did to-him these things, though he (is) of your-kind and you-had-kept-company-with-him a long period; and you-did-not spare him.
sentences.i: I have heard of you lately that you betrayed a companion of yours, the wolf, and plotted against him until your treachery and cunning destroyed him; you did all this to him, though he was of your own kind and you had been his companion a long while, and you showed him no mercy.
sentences.n: min qarīb, “from near”, lately. ghadara bi-, “to betray”, and makara bi-, “to plot against”: the verbs choose the bi-; in bi-ghadrika, “by your treachery”, it is instrumental, and in faʿala bihi, “to do to him”, it marks the one done to. هذة is the print's spelling of hādhihi. jins, “kind, species”: wolf and fox are of one kind. abqā ʿalā, “to spare”. The fatḥa on the b of صحبَته is the print's own and is kept, giving ṣaḥabtahu; Classical Arabic has ṣaḥibtahu, “you kept company with him”, and the print's vowel may be a misplaced one.

sentences.t: فَكَيْفَ أَثِقُ مِنْكَ بِنَصِيحَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-kayfa athiqu minka bi-naṣīḥatin
sentences.l: So how shall-I-trust from-you in counsel?
sentences.i: How then can I trust any counsel of yours?
sentences.n: wathiqa bi-, “to trust in, rely on”: the verb chooses the bi-; minka, “from you”, says whose counsel.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا فِعْلَكَ مَعَ صَاحِبِكَ الَّذِي مِنْ جِنْسِكَ فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ فِعْلُكَ مَعَ عَدُوِّكَ الَّذِي مِنْ غَيْرِ جِنْسِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā kāna hādhā fiʿlaka maʿa ṣāḥibika alladhī min jinsika fa-kayfa yakūnu fiʿluka maʿa ʿaduwwika alladhī min ghayri jinsika
sentences.l: And if this was your-doing with your-companion who (is) of your-kind, then how will-be your-doing with your-enemy who (is) of other-than your-kind?
sentences.i: If this is how you treat a companion of your own kind, how will you treat an enemy who is not of your kind?
sentences.n: kāna hādhā fiʿlaka, “this was your doing”: hādhā is the subject, fiʿlaka the predicate in the accusative. The shadda in عدوّك is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَمَا مِثَالُكَ مَعِي إِلَّا مِثَالُ الصَّقْرِ مَعَ ضَوَارِى الطَّيْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā mithāluka maʿī illā mithālu al-ṣaqri maʿa ḍawārī al-ṭayri
sentences.l: And not (is) your-likeness with-me except the likeness of the falcon with the ravening-ones of the birds.
sentences.i: You and I are like nothing so much as the falcon and the birds of prey.”
sentences.n: mā … illā, “is nothing but”. ṣaqr, “falcon, hawk”. ḍawārī, plural of ḍārī, “ravening, used to prey”: ḍawārī al-ṭayr, the birds of prey. The print writes its final -ī with ى. The likeness is only announced here; the crow's fable will explain it.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الثَّعْلَبُ وَكَيْفَ ذَلِكَ فَقَالَ الْغُرَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-thaʿlabu wa-kayfa dhālika fa-qāla al-ghurābu
sentences.l: And the fox said: And how (was) that? And the crow said:
sentences.i: The fox said, “And how was that?” The crow said:

sentences.t: زَعَمُوا أَنَّ صَقْرًا كَانَ جَبَّارًا عَنِيدًا
sentences.tr: zaʿamū anna ṣaqran kāna jabbāran ʿanīdan
sentences.l: They-claimed that a falcon was tyrannical, stubborn —
sentences.i: “They say that there was once a falcon, a tyrant, headstrong —
sentences.n: A new fable begins, the crow's answer to the fox. zaʿamū, “they claim”, the stock opening of a fable, as in Kalīla wa-Dimna. jabbār, “overbearing, tyrannical”; ʿanīd, “stubborn, refractory”. The shadda in جبّارا is the print's own. The sentence breaks off here, cut by the dawn; the next night takes it up.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
